beats.intro: Chapter two. [[sub]]How firms behave depends on how many rivals they have. We follow perfect competition, then monopoly.
beats.structures: [[a]]Economists sort markets into four structures. [[pc]]Perfect competition: many sellers, identical products, and no pricing power. [[mcm]]Monopolistic competition: many sellers, but differentiated products, so some pricing power. [[ol]]Oligopoly: a few sellers who watch each other's moves. [[mo]]Monopoly: a single seller, protected by barriers to entry, with the most pricing power.
beats.pc: [[a]]In perfect competition, buyers and sellers are many, and products are identical. [[mkt]]The market as a whole sets the price, where demand meets supply. [[firm]]Each firm is too small to move it. So a single firm faces a flat demand line at that price. It can sell as much as it likes at the going price, and nothing at a higher one.
beats.cs: [[a]]Consumer surplus is value minus expenditure. [[wtp]]The demand curve shows what each unit is worth to the buyer. [[price]]At a market price of four, the buyer pays four for every unit. [[cs]]The triangle between the demand curve and the price is consumer surplus: what buyers would have been willing to pay, less what they actually paid. [[fall]]Lower the price, and the surplus grows.
beats.firm: [[a]]A competitive firm can sell any amount at the market price, so marginal revenue equals price. [[mc]]It keeps adding output while marginal cost is below that price, and stops where they are equal. [[pt]]Here, that is about four units. [[prof]]Now compare price with average total cost at that output. The green rectangle is economic profit.
beats.longrun: [[a]]Economic profit attracts new firms. [[entry]]As they enter, market supply rises, and the price falls. [[end]]Entry stops when the price has fallen to the lowest point of average total cost. [[zero]]Economic profit is zero. Firms still earn a normal return on their capital, which is enough to stay. [[loss]]If price were lower, losses would push firms out, and the price would rise again.
beats.mdemand: [[a]]A monopolist is the only seller. It faces the whole market demand curve. [[d]]In the natural gas example, price equals eight hundred, minus two times quantity. [[mr]]To sell more, it must cut the price on every unit. So marginal revenue falls twice as fast: eight hundred minus four times quantity. [[half]]It reaches zero at two hundred units, halfway along the demand curve.
beats.mopt: [[a]]Marginal cost is fifty plus six times quantity. [[x]]The monopolist produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost: seventy-five units. [[p]]Then it reads the price from the demand curve: six hundred fifty. [[prof]]Average cost at that output is about five hundred forty-two, so profit is about one hundred eight per unit, and eight thousand one hundred twenty-five in total.
beats.dwl: [[a]]Compare this with perfect competition, where price equals marginal cost. [[c]]That would give about ninety-four units, at six hundred twelve fifty. [[m]]The monopolist makes fewer units, at a higher price. [[dwl]]The shaded triangle is deadweight loss: trades that would help both buyer and seller, but never happen. [[reg]]That is why regulators watch monopolies.
beats.disc: [[one]]With a single price, buyers who value the good more keep the extra as consumer surplus. [[more]]Charge different customers different prices, and the monopolist captures part of it. [[first]]First-degree: each customer pays the most they are willing to pay, so the seller takes all of the surplus. [[second]]Second-degree: a menu of quantity-based prices, such as volume discounts. [[third]]Third-degree: groups, such as students and businesses, are charged different prices.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Market structure runs from perfect competition to monopoly, by number of sellers and pricing power. [[w2]]A competitive firm takes the price, and produces where price equals marginal cost. [[w3]]In the long run, entry drives economic profit to zero. [[w4]]A monopolist sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost, reads its price off demand, and may price discriminate to capture surplus.
